title: I Never Knew You
paragraphs:
I Never Knew You
The Most Terrifying Words Jesus Ever Spoke—And Why They Might Not Mean What You Think
There are some verses in Scripture that comfort us.
And then there are verses that stop us cold.
Verses that feel like thunder rolling across a clear sky.
Verses that make even devoted churchgoers sit quietly for a moment and ask themselves questions they have spent years avoiding.
Few words in the entire Bible strike the human heart with more force than these:
“I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.”
For many people, these words have become a source of fear.
"What if Jesus says that to me?"
"What if I believed the wrong things?"
"What if all my efforts were meaningless?"
"What if I'm closer to God than ever... yet somehow still unknown by Him?"
Because what makes this passage so shocking is not who Jesus is speaking to.
It is who He is not speaking to.
He is not speaking to atheists.
Not people who openly rejected God.
The people standing before Him are religious.
Those five words reveal one of the most profound truths in all of Christianity.
The Gospel has never been primarily about religious activity.
It has always been about relationship.
The original Greek text makes this even more powerful.
The word translated "knew" is ἔγνων (egnōn) from γινώσκω (ginōskō).
This is not mere intellectual knowledge.
It does not mean recognizing someone's existence.
It speaks of intimate, personal, relational knowledge.
Throughout Scripture, knowing often refers to deep covenant relationship.
The same word used when Scripture says:
And suddenly the entire passage shifts.
Because the issue is not whether they did religious things.
The issue is whether they truly knew Christ and were known by Him.
Our culture is obsessed with appearances.
People can appear holy while secretly being exhausted.
Appear faithful while being spiritually empty.
Appear strong while carrying hidden rebellion.
Appear transformed while never truly surrendering.
He challenged people who honored God with their lips while their hearts remained distant.
He exposed external righteousness without internal transformation.
He challenged the illusion that outward activity equals inward surrender.
The frightening reality of Matthew 7 is that spiritual activity can sometimes become a substitute for intimacy with Christ.
A person can know theology and still not know Jesus.
They can attend church and still not know Jesus.
They can lead ministries and still not know Jesus.
They can quote Scripture and still not know Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about information.
It is about union with Christ.
This becomes even clearer when we examine the surrounding context.
Just before these famous words, Jesus says:
“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.”
In Hebrew culture, repetition often intensified meaning.
These people genuinely believed they belonged to Him.
The problem was never that they lacked religious language.
The problem was that they lacked transformed hearts.
This aligns perfectly with the message of the entire New Testament.
Salvation is not earned through works.
Yet genuine faith inevitably produces transformation.
A tree does not produce fruit in order to become alive.
It produces fruit because it already is alive.
Likewise, obedience is not the root of salvation.
It is the fruit of salvation.
Jesus is confronting people whose lives demonstrated no evidence of true surrender despite impressive spiritual appearances.
The phrase translated "workers of lawlessness" comes from the Greek:
ἀνομία (anomia) means lawlessness, rebellion, disregard for God's authority.
This is not describing imperfect believers struggling toward holiness.
This describes people whose lives remained fundamentally resistant to God's rule.
People who wanted His power but not His lordship.
His blessings but not His authority.
His miracles but not His mastery.
And if we are honest, this temptation remains alive today.
Yet Jesus offers both grace and transformation.
This is where the beauty of the Gospel explodes into view.
Because Matthew 7 is not merely a warning.
"Perform better and maybe God will love you."
"Christ loved you while you were still a sinner."
“But God shows His love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
That is the heartbeat of Christianity.
This is why our theme, From Scandal to Grace, captures the very essence of the Gospel.
Because every believer's story begins with scandal.
We all stand guilty before a holy God.
Yet Jesus enters the story and rewrites everything.
The cross becomes the place where scandal meets mercy.
Where sinners become sons and daughters.
The same Jesus who warns, “I never knew you,” is also the Jesus who says:
“Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.”
The people in Matthew 7 trusted their works.
The people welcomed by Christ trust Him.
One group points to what they did.
The other points to what He did.
Perhaps the greatest question is not:
When you fail, do you run toward Him rather than away from Him?
When He convicts you, do you repent?
When He calls, do you follow?
Because eternal life itself is defined by relationship.
“This is eternal life, that they know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.”
And maybe that is exactly why Matthew 7 remains so unforgettable.
If this message challenged your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
One day every title, platform, achievement, and applause will disappear, but being known by Jesus Christ will still be everything.
